sources.title: M. Visvesvaraya (Q741700), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-20): English description 'Indian engineer, scholar, statesman and the Diwan of Mysore (1861-1962)', instance of human, two birth values (15 September 1860 and 15 September 1861, the second with a reference), died 14 April 1962, no Korean label. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Aashique Ahmed Iqbal, 'India's Visionary Engineer', The India Forum (1 July 2025; read in full), a review by a historian at Krea University of Aparajith Ramnath's 'Engineering a Nation: The Life and Career of M. Visvesvaraya' (Penguin Viking, 2024). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: says he joined the Bombay Public Works Department in 1884, left after concluding he would not rise past a glass ceiling (he received the silver, not the gold, Kaisar-i-Hind medal in 1906), worked for princely states, in 1909 oversaw flood prevention in Hyderabad (which led to the Osman Sagar reservoir) and modernised its sanitation, as Diwan of Mysore (1912-1918) built the Krishnaraja Sagar dam against a resistant bureaucracy and the Madras government, pushed industrialisation (distillery and iron works that made no profit for decades) and an education policy more successful than any other diwan's, resigned in 1918 in a dispute with the Maharaja because he would not back the non-Brahmin movement, later headed the Bhadravati Iron and Steel Works and drafted policy papers on planning; Ramnath's argument is that his projects did not always succeed but showed India could industrialise, and the review notes critics who link his technocratic approach to environmental damage and rule by experts and calls the book comprehensive but sometimes easy on British policy. Scholarly review of the standard biography; the reviewer's summary, not the book itself.

Shubham Srivastav, review of Aparajith Ramnath's 'Engineering a Nation', Swarajya (2 March 2026; read in full). Second review of the same 708-page biography (so the same underlying source as the India Forum review): says he was cautious about publicly criticising the government early on and faced racial discrimination, was shaped by visits to Japan in the 1890s, chaired a Bombay conference condemning sedition-law arrests and drafted a 'Dominion Status for India' document, disagreed with Gandhi over heavy versus village industries, and advocated compulsory, women's and technical education and planning that encouraged collective effort without interfering with individual initiative; cites the economist D. R. Gadgil and the Marxist critic G. D. Parikh, who called his vision 'typically fascist' for supporting a citizen army. The review does not cover Sukkur, Hyderabad, Mysore or the dam.

Arun Mohan Sukumar, excerpt from 'Midnight's Machines: A Political History of Technology in India' (Penguin Viking), published by ThePrint on 14 December 2019 (read in full): as Mysore's chief engineer he conceived and supervised the Krishna Raja Sagara dam, India's largest river-valley project at the time, needing approval from the Maharaja, his diwan Ananda Rao, British officials (Viceroy Hardinge and the Resident) and the Madras Presidency, which had objected to a plan by his predecessor Captain Nicholas Dawes; he threatened to quit unless the Maharaja approved the dam and other pending projects, and the Maharaja relented; as Diwan (1912-1918) he backed the Allies in the First World War, sought provincial autonomy to direct money to industry, and saw a plan to bring Chrysler to Mysore blocked by the Government of India. Written by an author of a political history of technology; admiring of the engineer but critical of his politics. Reader comments below the page dispute how much credit he deserves, but are not part of the excerpt.

Arun Mohan Sukumar, 'Skilled engineer and planner, why M Visvesvaraya's ideas bit the dust post-Independence', The News Minute (12 December 2019; read in full), another excerpt of the same book as the ThePrint excerpt (so one source family): the Mysore Economic Conference he set up laid out annual public investment plans for the province; he moved sandalwood-oil extraction from the Indian Institute of Science into a soap factory; admired Meiji Japan; favoured state investment in large industry, public health and education; backed girls' education mainly for economic reasons, inter-caste marriage as a way to ease dowry demands, and rejected caste taboos on overseas travel; opposed denominational universities (disagreeing with Madan Mohan Malaviya) and differed from Gandhi on technology while keeping a cordial relationship; resigned as Diwan in protest over the Miller Committee on non-Brahmin government employment, which the author reads as resistance to affirmative action; ceded the chair of the National Planning Committee to Nehru and stopped attending after its second session. The author's argument is that his aversion to democratic politics left him sidelined.

Tenzin Zompa, 'M Visvesvaraya, the pioneer whose birthday India celebrates on 15 Sept as Engineers' Day', ThePrint (15 September 2021, updated to reflect the views of the scholar Chandan Gowda; read in full): born into a poor Brahmin family, lost his father at 15 and tutored children to continue studying, took a BA at Central College in 1881; designed a flood protection system for Hyderabad, the block system of irrigation, and introduced automatic sluice gates on dams; chief engineer to Mysore in 1909, Diwan in 1912; says he set up 6,500 new schools and drafted legislation for compulsory primary education in his first six years as Diwan (an unsourced figure); resigned over the Miller Committee, which critics read as protecting upper-caste privilege, while Gowda disputes calling him casteist and describes him as a liberal gradualist who saw caste inequality mainly as an economic problem. Journalism leaning on one expert's interpretation; the article gives no dates for the dam or the Hyderabad scheme.

'Sir M. Visvesvaraya: An Excellent Statesman and Eminent Engineer', karnataka.com (general-interest Karnataka website, undated, no author; read in full). Compiled biography, weakest source here: lists his 1884 start as assistant engineer in the Bombay service, automatic weir floodgates first at Khadakvasla near Pune in 1903 and later at Tigra and the Krishna Raja Sagar dam, the block system, Hyderabad flood protection (chief engineer of Hyderabad for seven months in 1909), chief engineer of Mysore from November 1909, voluntary retirement in 1908 followed by a tour of industrialised countries, and a long list of enterprises and institutions of his Diwanship from 1912 (soap factory, iron and steel works at Bhadravati, bank, university, polytechnic, engineering college, chambers of commerce); calls him sincere, punctual and disciplined (unsourced). It has internal inconsistencies (for example a centenary stamp issued in 1960 for a man it says was born in 1861) and cites no primary sources, so it is used only to corroborate offices, projects and dates reported elsewhere.

Swarajya Staff, 'How M. Visvesvaraya Made Hyderabad Flood-Free: Lessons for Smart Cities', Swarajya (2 April 2016; read in full), excerpts from his own autobiography 'Memoirs of My Working Life' (so partly self-report): after the cyclonic flood of 28 September 1908, which reportedly drowned about two thousand people at Kolsawadi, he arrived in Hyderabad on 15 April 1909, submitted a flood protection report on 1 October, a reservoir report on 20 October and a sewerage outline on 6 November, and left the service in November; proposed storage reservoirs on the Musi and its tributary the Easi above the city (about 20,389 million cubic feet), raised river banks turned into walks and gardens, and diverted sewage to a separate farm; the Musi reservoir foundation stone was laid in March 1913, he was invited back to advise on drainage in 1922 and submitted a report in 1930; names the engineers who built the dams and thanks the Hyderabad minister Akbar Hydari. His own account of his work; the other sources confirm the broad outline.

Gouri Satya, 'KRS Dam: Setting the record straight', Star of Mysore (7 August 2025; read in full). Local newspaper feature on a dispute about who founded the dam (a minister had claimed Tipu Sultan laid its foundation): says construction began in 1911 and finished about twenty years later entirely under the reign of Maharaja Krishnaraja Wadiyar IV, who gave the patronage, funding and administrative support, and that Visvesvaraya was the planner and designer. Useful for the shared credit for the dam and for the fact that the work continued long after he left office in 1918; not a source on his conduct.

persistence.rationale: [src_mv_sukumar_prt, src_mv_iqbal, src_mv_karnataka, src_mv_starmysore | 1909-1918 | book excerpt, book review, general-interest web biography, local newspaper feature] The dam excerpt describes him pushing the Kaveri project through approval by the Maharaja, the diwan, British officials and the Madras Presidency, which had objected to an earlier plan; the review adds friction with a resistant bureaucracy and the Madras government. The Star of Mysore says construction began in 1911 and ended about twenty years later, so he was not in office at completion. Persistence is shown in the fight for approval, not in finishing the work. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 74 / 0.60 to 68 / 0.52 because the sources reduce to one author's book, the review of another biography and a web compilation, and credit for the dam is shared with the Maharaja.

persuasiveness.rationale: [src_mv_sukumar_prt, src_mv_sukumar_tnm, src_mv_iqbal | 1909-1914 | book excerpts, book review] Sukumar records approvals he obtained for the dam from the Maharaja, the diwan, British officials and the Madras Presidency, and his setting up of the annual Mysore Economic Conference to lay out investment plans; the review notes friction with the bureaucracy. The Maharaja relented after he threatened to resign, which is leverage as much as persuasion, and both excerpts are one author. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.54 strong_inference to 62 / 0.46 inference because the approvals rest on one author and one of the two key episodes is a resignation threat.

planning_orientation.rationale: [src_mv_sukumar_tnm, src_mv_iqbal, src_mv_memoir_swarajya, src_mv_prt2021 | 1909-1930s | book excerpt, book review, memoir excerpts, news article] The Mysore Economic Conference he set up laid out annual public investment plans (Sukumar); in Hyderabad in 1909 he submitted flood protection, reservoir and sewerage reports in sequence over about seven months (his memoir, as excerpted); the review says he later drafted many policy documents on constitution-making and economic planning; ThePrint says he drafted legislation for compulsory primary education. The plans are well attested, but part of the evidence is his own memoir and implementation was mixed (the review says the Mysore ventures made no profit for decades). CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 74 / 0.58 to 72 / 0.54 because the sequence of reports is his own account and the conference plans rest on one author.

systems_abstraction.rationale: [src_mv_memoir_swarajya, src_mv_iqbal, src_mv_karnataka | 1909 | memoir excerpts, book review, general-interest web biography] His Hyderabad scheme combined storage reservoirs above the city on the Musi and Easi, raised river banks turned into walks and gardens, and a separate sewage farm to reduce pollution (his memoir, as excerpted), and the review says he also modernised the city's sanitation. This shows a multi-part urban water scheme, but the detail comes from his own account and no source describes how he reasoned about systems. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.52 strong_inference to 64 / 0.48 inference because the scheme's content is self-reported.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_mv_iqbal, src_mv_karnataka, src_mv_sukumar_tnm, src_mv_prt2021 | 1908-1918 | book review, general-interest web biography, book excerpt, news article] The review says he left the Bombay service after concluding he would not rise further and worked for princely states; the web biography adds a voluntary retirement in 1908 and a tour of industrialised countries. As Diwan he is credited with the Mysore Economic Conference, the soap factory (Sukumar), and with a list of institutions including the university, the bank, the iron and steel works and an engineering college (web biography, ThePrint), which the review frames as an industrialisation push. Several initiatives are well attested, but credit for each is shared with the Maharaja and the founding lists come from a weak compilation. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 76 / 0.60 to 72 / 0.54 because shared credit cannot be separated and the longest list is the weakest source.

opportunity_sensing.rationale: [src_mv_sukumar_tnm, src_mv_sukumar_prt, src_mv_iqbal | 1912-1918 | book excerpts, book review] Sukumar says he moved sandalwood-oil extraction from the Indian Institute of Science into a soap factory and tried to bring Chrysler to Mysore for a car plant (blocked by the Government of India); the review says the distillery and iron works he pushed made no profit for decades. Spotting openings is documented, outcomes were mixed, and both excerpts are one author, hence a near-neutral inference. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.46 to 58 / 0.40 because the evidence is one author's examples and the commercial results were weak, which makes the sensing hard to separate from the outcome.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_mv_iqbal, src_mv_prt2021, src_mv_sukumar_tnm | 1909-1918 | book review, news article, book excerpt] The review says his career was driven by a belief that state-led industrialisation would end starvation and poverty; ThePrint says he set up 6,500 schools in his first six years as Diwan (an unsourced figure) and drafted compulsory primary-education legislation; Sukumar adds that he supported girls' education mainly for economic reasons. The purpose is the reviewers' reading of his choices and his published views, not an independent record of his motives. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.54 strong_inference to 64 / 0.46 inference because the motive is attributed by a reviewer and the school figure is unsourced.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_mv_sukumar_prt, src_mv_sukumar_tnm, src_mv_iqbal, src_mv_prt2021 | 1909-1918 | book excerpts, book review, news article] Sukumar says he threatened to quit unless the Maharaja approved the dam and other pending projects; the review describes clashes with a resistant bureaucracy and the Madras government over the Kaveri and says he resigned as Diwan in 1918 in a dispute with the Maharaja over the non-Brahmin movement; Sukumar and ThePrint tie the resignation to the Miller Committee, and accounts of his motive differ (resistance to affirmative action versus merit and efficiency). The confrontations are documented and the 1918 resignation cost him the office, so the impact is dual-edged. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.54 to 64 / 0.50 because the resignation threat is single-source and the motive of the resignation is contested.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_mv_sukumar_tnm, src_mv_prt2021, src_mv_srivastav | 1910s-1940 | book excerpt, news article, book review] Sukumar lists positions at odds with prominent contemporaries: disagreement with Gandhi over technology, opposition to denominational universities against Malaviya, and opposition to the Miller Committee; ThePrint adds that he viewed religious belief as an obstacle to rational thought, and the Swarajya review that he disagreed with Gandhi over heavy versus village industry. Dissent is documented, but it is one author's list and the review notes his early caution in public criticism of government. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.46 to 62 / 0.42 because the list rests on one author and his public caution tempers it.

portrait.reason: HOLD (portrait). No portrait with a verified holder record and a clear reuse basis was found. (1) Rashtrapati Bhavan 1955 photograph 'Dr. M. Visveswarayya receiving the Bharat Ratna award from President Dr. Prasad' (Commons file, tagged GODL-India, unreviewed, author unknown, 2000 x 1390): the live holder page is dead (old domain); the Internet Archive copy of the holder's 1955 gallery (2023-05-27) lists the photograph with that caption, but the same site's Copyright Policy (archived 2023) says its contents should not be reproduced without due permission from Rashtrapati Bhavan while its Terms and Conditions say material may be reproduced free of charge with acknowledgment (excluding third-party material), neither mentions the Government Open Data License, no item-level rights statement or photographer exists, and a 1955 Indian government photograph would not be public domain in the United States by age. The GODL-India tag therefore rests on an unreviewed Commons assertion. (2) 'Who's Who in India, Burma and Ceylon' 1937 portrait (Commons 'Sir Mokshagundam Vishveshwaraiya.jpg'): published 1937, not public domain in the United States, Indian-origin copyright restored. (3) 'Vishveshvarayya in his 30's' (c. 1890, Commons, source indiannerve.com, author unknown): no publication chain or holder. (4) Pre-1931 books checked for a frontispiece portrait: Visvesvaraya, Speeches (Bangalore Government Press, 1917, Internet Archive VisvesvarayaSpeeches) and Reconstructing India (London, King, 1920, Internet Archive reconstructingin00visvuoft) carry no portrait plate in their opening pages. (5) 1960 India stamp: Indian government work published 1960, restored in the United States. No other person was substituted.

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: RISKY (Stage B) / lead did NOT survive: the Rashtrapati Bhavan 1955 Bharat Ratna photograph exists in the holder's 1955 gallery (Internet Archive copy of 2023) but the holder's Copyright Policy and Terms conflict, no GODL statement or photographer is given, and the US status is unfavourable; the replacement routes (1937 Who's Who, c. 1890 web image, pre-1931 books, 1960 stamp) failed or carried no portrait, so portrait is held and the candidate stays portrait_pending (portrait-only blocker; evidence is complete). PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE (2026-11-20, Wikidata API) Q741700 label 'M. Visvesvaraya', description 'Indian engineer, scholar, statesman and the Diwan of Mysore (1861-1962)', human, died 1962-04-14; Wikidata carries two birth values (1860 normal rank, 1861 referenced); BIRTH YEAR 1861 is used because the reviewed biography, the Wikidata description and most sources give 1861 (the frozen list had 1860); no Korean Wikidata label or Korean Wikipedia article. REGION south_asia. ERA 20th_century (career 1884-1950s, main works 1903-1930s; birth 1861). Nationality IN. ZERO POLITICS (where possible): scored only engineering, planning, institution-building and workplace conduct; the Miller Committee resignation is used only as a documented dispute with his employer and is not scored as a stance on caste reservation, his National Planning Committee withdrawal and his views on socialism, nationalism and the British are context and unscored, and the Diwan title is carried as an administrative office (the occupation is engineer only, not statesman). KOREAN NAME: transliteration (no Korean usage found): 모크샤군담 비슈베슈와라야, following the Korean standard spelling for Hindi-derived names (as in 비슈누); flagged for lead review. ATTRIBUTION: attributable (extensive documentary record of dated projects, offices and publications), but credit for the dam is shared with the Maharaja and others and the Hyderabad detail is self-reported. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Iqbal, The India Forum review of Ramnath's biography. READ (8 sources besides Wikidata, all in full): Iqbal review; Srivastav review of the same biography; Sukumar excerpts in ThePrint and The News Minute (same book); ThePrint 2021; karnataka.com; Swarajya memoir excerpts on Hyderabad; Star of Mysore. Not read: Ramnath's book, Visvesvaraya's own memoir in full (the NEHU repository copy was unreachable), the ICE page (it returned a page that gives the KRS appointment as 1924, a clear error, and was not cited), Britannica (not found), Wikipedia. PERSPECTIVES: academic review of the standard biography; second review of the same book; political-history excerpts critical of his politics; journalism with a scholar's reading of the caste dispute; compiled web biography; his own memoir via a newspaper excerpt; a local newspaper on credit for the dam. NON-SELF BEHAVIOURAL SOURCES: the two reviews, the Sukumar excerpts and ThePrint 2021 (the memoir excerpt is self-report). CONTRADICTIONS AND LIMITS: birth year 1860 vs 1861; the web biography places a 1960 centenary stamp against an 1861 birth; construction of the dam began 1911 and ended about twenty years later (Star of Mysore) while he left office in 1918, so no completion claim is carded; credit to the Maharaja and to Captain Dawes appears in reader comments and the local article; the iron works and distillery were unprofitable for decades (review); the cause of his 1918 resignation is read differently by Sukumar, ThePrint's critics and Gowda; the school count (6,500) is unsourced; ICE's 1924 date is wrong. SPARSE PROFILE BY DESIGN: 9 rows; no discipline row (punctuality and discipline appear only in the weak web compilation), no creative originality row (invention credits for the gates and the block system rest on press summaries), no risk row (the 1908 retirement is thinly documented).
